payload.rationale: The event requires the seasonally adjusted headline CPI monthly change for November 2026 (released Dec 10, 2026) to print 0.3% or higher at one decimal. Observed facts: 2026 monthly headline prints have been volatile (0.3, 0.9, 0.6, 0.5, -0.4, 0.1, 0.4 from Feb–Aug), August core was 0.3%, twelve-month headline inflation is 3.4%, and September FOMC projections put 2026 PCE inflation at 3.7% and core PCE at 3.4% — an elevated inflation regime. A 3.4% annual pace implies an average monthly headline of roughly 0.28%, so the 0.3% threshold sits near the center of the plausible distribution; in past periods with inflation running 3–4% annually, prints of 0.3% or more occurred somewhat more than half the time, while energy swings (as in June's -0.4%) produced frequent misses. With core apparently running around 0.3% monthly, headline exceeding 0.2% is roughly a coin flip tilted slightly toward yes. Too high: an oil/gasoline decline in October–November, easing shelter, or the Fed's still-restrictive stance (policy ~4.1%) could pull headline to 0.1–0.2%, and the Aug gasoline jump (3.9%) could partially reverse. Too low: if the recent surge (Mar–May) reflects persistent tariff or supply pressure and core stays at 0.3%+, headline prints of 0.3–0.5% could be the norm, making yes considerably more likely than 50%. No October/November data, commodity outlook, or component model is available, so the estimate leans on regime-level base rates.
limitations: October and November 2026 price data and energy price trajectories are unobserved.
Estimate relies on rough historical base rates for monthly prints in a ~3.4% inflation regime, not a fitted component model.
PCE projections are a different index and annual, not monthly CPI; one-decimal rounding around the 0.25% boundary adds sensitivity.
Possible release delays or revisions to seasonal factors could affect settlement timing or value.
